column1: In song structure, what are the three distinct jobs handled by verse, chorus, and bridge?
column2: Verse delivers new lyric information over familiar harmony/melody; chorus strips the song to its most repeatable, singable, highest-energy core; bridge deliberately breaks the pattern to make the final chorus hit harder.

column1: What melodic range and motion should a verse melody stay within, and why?
column2: A 6th to an octave range, mostly stepwise motion. Reaching wider or leaping more means you're accidentally writing chorus material — big leaps also force singers to 'aim,' breaking flow across changing lyrics.

column1: How should a verse typically end harmonically, and why?
column2: On something that wants to move — a V chord (half cadence) or a I chord with rhythmic push — never a dead stop, because the verse's job is to create momentum into the chorus.

column1: What are the three phonological categories of consonants/vowels in lyric writing, and their singing behavior?
column2: Open vowels (ah, oh, ee mid-range) sustain long notes/high pitches without strain; plosives (p,t,k,b,d,g) stop airflow and land like percussion hits (good for rhythm, bad for sustain); fricatives (s,f,sh,v) hiss and sustain tension but can't carry pitch center; nasals (m,n,ng) resonate and blend into legato lines.

column1: Why do closed vowels (like 'ih' or tight 'oo') cause problems on high/belted notes?
column2: High notes require an open, unobstructed vocal tract; closed vowels narrow the throat and mouth exactly when maximum opening is needed, causing strain, pitch flatting, or pinched tone — this is vocal tract acoustics, not just taste.

column1: What is 'prosodic mapping' in lyric writing and why does mismatching it sound wrong?
column2: It's aligning a word's natural English stress pattern (content words stressed, function words unstressed) with the music's strong-beat grid. When the two stress grids clash, listeners register 'wrong' before they can explain why.

column1: What is Rule 1 of melodic coherence regarding steps vs. leaps?
column2: Steps dominate (65–75% of melodic motion is stepwise), and leaps get 'repaid' — over 75% of the time, a leap is followed by motion back toward its starting point or filled in stepwise in the opposite direction.

column1: What is Rule 2 of melodic coherence regarding scale degrees and rest?
column2: Scale degrees carry different levels of tension: ending a phrase on the tonic (1̂) sounds closed/finished, while ending on the leading tone (7̂) or supertonic (2̂) sounds like an unresolved question — letting you engineer exactly how 'finished' a phrase feels.

column1: Why do large melodic leaps (above a 7th) feel dramatic or disruptive?
column2: Auditory streaming — the brain's process of tracking which notes belong to one melodic line — breaks down above roughly a 7th, so the brain briefly loses the thread and must work to re-attach it.

column1: What are the three practical acoustic facts underlying functional harmony in songwriting?
column2: 1) The perfect fifth (3:2 ratio) is the strongest consonance after the octave, making V→I progressions feel solid. 2) The tritone (e.g., B–F in a G7 chord) is the most unstable interval, resolving by both notes stepping inward. 3) Equal temperament spreads tuning error evenly across all keys, allowing free modulation on fixed-pitch instruments.

column1: In a minor key, why swap the v minor chord for V major when writing a cadence?
column2: Natural minor's v chord (e.g., Em in A minor) lacks a leading tone and resolves softly. Raising the 7th to form V major (E major, with G♯) creates a true leading tone (G♯→A) that pulls hard and resolves strongly to the tonic.

column1: What is the functional difference between an authentic cadence (V→I), a half cadence (ending on V), and a deceptive cadence (V→vi)?
column2: Authentic cadence (V→I) sounds finished, like a period — used for choruses/endings. Half cadence (ending on V) sounds like a comma, creating forward momentum — ideal for verse endings. Deceptive cadence (V→vi) sounds like a left turn, used to extend a phrase or avoid early resolution.
